Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War is a military science fiction real-time strategy video game developed by Relic Entertainment and based on Games Workshop's miniature wargame Warhammer 40,000. It was released by THQ on September 20, 2004, in North America and on September 24 in Europe.

Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. Three expansion packs have been released: Winter Assault in 2005, Dark Crusade in 2006, and Soulstorm in 2008. A remastered version of the game and its three expansions, titled Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War - Definitive Edition, was released on August 14, 2025.

The honest version of Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War starts by giving up the comforting part. The game has three sequels: Dawn of War II (2009), Dawn of War III (2017), and Dawn of War IV (2026). Gameplay is initially focused on capturing and holding strategic locations on the battlefield.

Strip Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. These control points are captured by infantry squads and provide resources to construct additional units and buildings or unlock certain units in an army's tech tree. Battles are won either by holding a certain number of control points for a period of time or by destroying all of the opposing armies' HQ structures.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War shows exactly where that breaks. A number of special conditions are available to choose from to customize matches. The game is set in the Warhammer 40,000 universe: a dystopian vision of the far future in which humanity has forged a galaxy-spanning empire, The Imperium of Man.

What looks like free choice in Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War is older than choice itself. The story of this campaign also sets the stage for the events of Dawn of War II - Retribution. The Blood Ravens' Space Marines, upon descent to the planet's surface, secure Tartarus' spaceport and start their own operations against the warring Orkish forces.

Nobody designed the part of Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War you experience — it was inherited. Unknown to the Space Marines, however, the Orks' invasion was in fact engineered by the Chaos Alpha Legion's Sorcerer, Sindri Myr, as a smokescreen to their operations on Tartarus, using the forces of Sindri's supposed commander, Lord Bale.

Every serious account of Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. The Librarian, however, secretly harbours Chaos artifacts and he damages the Blood Ravens' transports to allow further research time, being influenced constantly by Sindri's temptations.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Angelos' forces track the Eldar to the urban settlement of Loovre Marr, engaging them in full-scale battle, as Sindri and the Alpha Legion infiltrate the city and abscond with an artifact, which Macha believes is the "key to the undoing of this world". Angelos clashes again with Toth, who assumes command of all of the planet's Imperial assets, except the Blood Ravens and 37th Tartarus Planetary Defence Force, after learning Angelos employed Colonel Brom's Imperial Guard to assist him.

The selfish-gene reading of Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War makes it less romantic and far more precise. Toth claims that Angelos' stubbornness to leave the planet may be a sign of Chaos corruption. Toth explains that the Eldar presence on Tartarus was to prevent the Alpha Legion from unearthing the stone, unwilling to inform or cooperate with Imperial forces due to arrogant behaviour, seeing themselves as "the only capable defence against its influence".

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. Angelos and Toth make amends and advance against the primary position of the Alpha Legion, as it is performing an unholy ritual to unearth the Maledictum. However, while the Blood Ravens and the remaining loyal Imperial Guard exterminate Lord Bale's forces, the same abandoned by Sindri to die to unearth the artifact, Isador takes the Maledictum and departs with Sindri, revealing that he had been overcome by the temptations of Chaos.

The feeling that Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. Angelos and Toth pursue  but only reach him after he has been subdued by Sindri who takes the Maledictum. As the Blood Ravens destroy Isador's Chaos forces, Angelos fights Isador in a hand-to-hand duel.

Nothing in Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War was built for you — it was built for reproduction. Despite Isador's taunts of Gabriel's supposed weakness and guilt for the events of Cyrene, Gabriel overcomes them, citing "innocents must die so that humanity may live", implying that the planet was long corrupted by Chaos and there was no salvation but by destruction. Defeating Isador, Angelos executes him even as the Librarian tries pleading for forgiveness.

The psychology underneath Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War is simpler and older than the story on top. Angelos and Toth chase Sindri to a ritual site, as the Warp Storm approaches, but fail to apprehend him before he performs a ritual with the Maledictum to sacrifice himself in order to summon a Daemon Prince. As Toth bequeaths his Daemon Hammer, "God-Splitter", to Angelos, the Blood Ravens, assisted by the Eldar survivors, fight and overcome the remaining Alpha Legion in a violent battle, overcoming the Daemon Prince despite its power.

Behind Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. In the aftermath, Toth orders Angelos to destroy the Maledictum, while Macha pleads him to stay his hammer. As all parties start to evacuate, Angelos is called back and faces the daemon that he has unknowingly freed from its prison, the Maledictum.

The nihilist does not deny Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War — he only refuses to flatter it. It is implied that had the Blood Ravens realized this and destroyed the Maledictum earlier, the daemon would likely have been destroyed as well. The daemon allows Angelos and the Blood Ravens to leave, though with a message that he soon would be coming for them all.

What culture calls destiny in Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. Gabriel vows to destroy the daemon, stating "I know you now", before finally departing Tartarus. The base game has three expansions, all available in retail DVD format and via digital distribution.

Take away the meaning and Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War still functions — that is the disturbing part. In chronological order of release, these expansions are: Winter Assault, Dark Crusade and Soulstorm. Out of these, Winter Assault requires the base game whereas the other two are stand-alone.

The bleak reading of Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War is also the most testable one. The "Master Collection" on Steam and GOG.com, similar to "The Complete Collection", includes the "Game of the Year Edition" of the game as well as the three expansions. The "Anniversary Edition" replaced the "Master Collection" as a single package on Steam and GOG.com as of September 19, 2024 to commemorate the 20th anniversary of the original game.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War. Owners of the original game were upgraded to the "Anniversary Edition" for free. A definitive edition of the game was released on August 15, 2025.

The self that experiences Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War is a committee, not a king. It consists of a bundle of the base game and its expansion packs, alongside graphical and gameplay improvements. By early 2009, Dawn of War and its expansion packs together had sold 4 million copies.

Reproduction explains more of Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War than any philosophy dares to admit. Dawn of War received a "Silver" sales award from the Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association (ELSPA), indicating sales of at least 100,000 copies in the United Kingdom. Upon release, the critical response to Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War was on the whole positive.

Once you see Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. It was congratulated most frequently for its varied and balanced factions and units, its polished presentation, in particular the high quality of unit animations, and the user interface. One of the first reviews was by IGN, who awarded the game 8.8/10, in particular praising the large level of graphical and animation detail.

The story Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. GameSpot came to similar conclusions, in particular praising the game's presentation and audio. Conversely, an area of the game that drew criticism was the single player campaign, which many reviewers found to be too short and unchallenging.

Meaning is not found in Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War — it is manufactured for it. Another area of weakness identified was a lack of originality in the gameplay. German reviewer Daniel Matschijewsky awarded the game 83 out of 100, praising the user interface and the sound, but identifying the campaign and the AI as weaker areas.
